description: Rocketry Creations is Leo Yim's team for the 2026 NASA Space Apps Challenge at the Irvine Virtual event, working on "Ba An Earth System Trend Detective!"
summary:
Winds at Two Heights is a project that investigates how wind speeds change over time, across locations, and at different heights in the atmosphere. We combined NASA POWER/MERRA-2 atmospheric data with real measurements collected from three rocket launches at El Mirage, California.

Our project analyzes historical wind-speed data from 1981 to 2025 at 10 and 50 meters above the ground in Irvine and El Mirage. We developed visualizations, trend graphs, and statistical analyses to identify long-term changes and evaluate their significance.

We also incorporated a rocket payload equipped with wind, temperature, pressure, and GPS sensors to demonstrate how atmospheric measurements can be collected during flight.

Our project addresses NASA's Earth System Trend Detective challenge by using Earth science data to investigate environmental patterns. By combining rocket engineering with NASA climate data, we hope to make atmospheric science more accessible, interactive, and engaging for students while encouraging further environmental research.
details:
What Our Project Does

Our project, Winds at Two Heights, investigates how wind speeds have changed over time at different heights and locations in Southern California. We wanted to understand whether wind patterns are changing and how NASA's Earth science data can help us identify long-term trends.

We analyzed NASA POWER/MERRA-2 atmospheric data from 1981 to 2025, comparing wind speeds at 10 meters and 50 meters above the ground in Irvine and El Mirage, California.

We created graphs showing annual wind-speed changes and calculated trends in meters per second per decade. We also examined statistical significance using p-values to determine whether the observed trends provide evidence of long-term changes.

Our Rocket Payload

A unique part of our project is our real rocket-based atmospheric data collection system.

We used an experimental rocket payload containing sensors for wind-related measurements, air pressure, temperature, and GPS positioning. We collected data during three rocket launches at El Mirage, California, on July 5, 2026.

The rocket records allow us to examine atmospheric conditions during flight and visualize the rocket's altitude and trajectory. We included a 3D flight-path replay to demonstrate how atmospheric measurements can be collected at different altitudes.

Our rocket measurements complement NASA's historical data. Because the rocket flights occurred on a single day, they cannot independently establish long-term climate trends.

Our Findings

Our analysis of the NASA modeled wind data indicates that estimated average wind speeds decreased over the study period at both locations and both heights.

Irvine showed stronger estimated decreases than El Mirage. We also found that some trends were more statistically significant than others, demonstrating why statistical analysis is important when interpreting environmental data.

Tools and Technology

Our project uses:

  • NASA POWER/MERRA-2 historical atmospheric datasets.
  • Rocket-based wind, temperature, and pressure sensors.
  • GPS for recording rocket position and altitude.
  • Data visualization and statistical analysis software.
  • Time-series graphs and linear trend analysis.
  • A 3D rocket flight visualization.
  • A video demonstration presenting our methods and findings.

Creativity and Benefits

Our project combines real rocket engineering with NASA Earth science data analysis.

Instead of only looking at historical climate graphs, we connect large-scale atmospheric datasets with measurements from a student-built rocket payload.

This approach helps make Earth science more interesting and understandable for students. It also demonstrates how engineering, programming, mathematics, and environmental science can work together.

Challenges and Considerations

We considered sensor accuracy, missing rocket telemetry, differences between modeled atmospheric data and direct measurements, and the importance of separating short-term weather observations from long-term trends.

We also considered how rocket motion can influence airflow measurements and why additional calibration is necessary to estimate true atmospheric wind speeds.

Intended Impact and Future Development

Our goal is to encourage students to explore atmospheric science using both NASA data and hands-on experiments.

In the future, we hope to conduct additional rocket flights, improve our wind-sensor calibration, and compare rocket measurements with atmospheric models at corresponding altitudes and times.

Ultimately, we want to demonstrate how accessible technology and publicly available NASA data can help students investigate changes in Earth's atmosphere.
